title: a path
hook: a path — eight parts, a life
tomorrow: mindfulness before it was a corporate wellness word

segments.voice: Yesterday: the third truth, nirodha, the flame going out. Your line was there is an end. Did you notice something hard actually ending? Day eight.

Think of the last time someone told you what was wrong, and then just left. A mechanic who says your car has a problem and walks off. A friend who says you seem stressed, and changes the subject. It's worse than not knowing. The first three truths could have been like that. There is dukkha. It comes from thirst. It can end. Great. How? The Buddha didn't leave it there. The fourth truth isn't an idea at all. It's directions. And they aren't a one-time fix, like a pill. They're something you walk, every day, for a life.
screen: `THE PROBLEM, THEN SILENCE.` → `GREAT. HOW?` → `THE FOURTH TRUTH IS DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: The fourth noble truth is magga, the path. The way that leads to the end of dukkha. It has eight parts, so it's called the noble eightfold path. Here they are, quickly. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. The word translated right is samma, and it's gentler than it sounds in English. It means whole, complete, well-tuned, the way a chord is right. Not right as opposed to wrong answers on a test. Right the way a thing fits. Later teachers grouped the eight into three bundles. Wisdom: seeing clearly and meaning well. Conduct: how you speak, act and earn a living. And meditation: effort, mindfulness, concentration. Notice what that means. Half the path isn't sitting on a cushion. It's how you talk to your sister and how you make your money. And here's the key thing people get wrong. The eight aren't steps you finish one at a time, like levels. They're more like the eight spokes of a wheel, which is why the wheel is the symbol of the teaching. They turn together. A little honesty helps meditation. A little meditation helps honesty. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says it plainly: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words." The four words are the four truths you now know. And the eightfold way is how you walk them. Not believe them. Walk them.
screen: `MAGGA — THE PATH.` · `EIGHT PARTS, EACH ONE SAMMA.` · `WISDOM, CONDUCT, MEDITATION.` · `SPOKES OF A WHEEL, NOT STEPS.` · then, large: `THE BEST OF WAYS IS THE EIGHTFOLD.`

segments.voice: Today the bell gives you a little longer: about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. Pick just one spoke of the wheel for today. Maybe speech: one thing you'll say more kindly. Maybe action: one small harm you'll skip. Maybe livelihood: one moment at work you'll do honestly. Hold that one spoke in mind, and breathe with it. You don't have to walk all eight today. One step is still walking. The bell holds the time.
The fourth. The fourth noble truth, magga: an eightfold path, wisdom, conduct and meditation, turning together like a wheel. Eighth word.
Your line: walk. Today, take the spoke you picked and actually use it once, in a real conversation or a real choice. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MINDFULNESS BEFORE IT WAS A CORPORATE WELLNESS WORD.`

howItsDone: Buddhists practice the eightfold path as a whole way of life: keeping ethical precepts in speech, action and work, meditating, and studying the teaching; the eight-spoked wheel, the dharmachakra, is one of Buddhism's most common symbols.

fork.setup: you want to start the eightfold path today. where do you begin?
options: right view. you can't do the rest until it's perfect.
right concentration. meditation first, life later.
fork.reveal: the eight parts support each other like spokes. many teachers say you can start anywhere: a little honesty helps meditation, and a little meditation helps honesty.

original.note: Pali: the noble eightfold path. magga, path; aṭṭhaṅgika, eight-limbed.

trapdoor: what you thought: eight rules to follow.
what it means: eight parts of one path, wisdom, conduct and meditation, practiced together for a life.
what a scholar hears: ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga. the threefold grouping into paññā, sīla and samādhi is given by the nun Dhammadinnā in the Culavedalla Sutta (MN 44).
